scope_notes: Covers posture in closed guard (top), guard retention / hip escape (shrimp), trap-and-roll (upa) mount escape, armbar from closed guard, triangle choke, guard passing fundamentals and the technical stand-up. Leg locks are covered only as a safety note.
source_gap_notes: Fewer than 10 strong technique sources: peer-reviewed BJJ research is mostly injury epidemiology plus one armlock kinematics study; technique cues come from Gracie University, John Danaher (via BJJ Fanatics/BJJ Universe summaries) and Grapplearts. Many top instructionals are paywalled, so only public summaries were used. Video analysis of BJJ is harder for 2D pose models (two entangled bodies, gi occlusion).

skills.name: Guard retention and hip escape (shrimp)
skills.recommended_camera: Side view at mat level, perpendicular to the athletes.

checkpoints.description: Frame before moving: sit up or turn to your side and use the skeleton (a straight arm, elbow or shoulder, with the hand/elbow planted at the right angle) so bones, not muscles, carry the passer's weight.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: shoulder line tilted > ~45 deg from the mat (on side); framing elbow extended

checkpoints.description: Hip escape: bring the feet back toward the hips, plant them, and drive the hips backward away from the passer (a backward shrimp) to create space.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: hip midpoint moves away from the passer by > ~1 hip-width while shoulders stay roughly in place

checkpoints.description: Re-insert a knee, shin or foot hook between you and the passer to recover guard.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: a knee/shin occupies the space between chests within ~1 s after the hip escape

checkpoints.description: Danaher's principles: keep head above the hips when seated, maintain connection with knees/elbows, manage distance and use frames.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: seated: head above hips; knees and elbows close (connected) to protect the chest

faults.name: Flat on the back
faults.video_signs: Both shoulders on the mat, facing the ceiling; passer lands chest-to-chest.
faults.correction_cue: 'Get on your side - frame and shrimp.'
faults.why_it_matters: Flat positions remove the ability to frame and move the hips.

faults.name: Shrimping toward the pressure / without frames
faults.video_signs: Hips move but toward the passer, or frames collapse so space closes again.
faults.why_it_matters: Without frames, any space created is immediately taken back.

drills.name: Solo shrimp line drill
drills.setup: Lie on the mat at one end of a lane.
steps: Solo shrimps down the mat, alternating sides.
Grapplearts 'elbow shrimp' and 'hand shrimp': sit up on an elbow or hand frame, plant the feet, hip-escape backward.
Partner progression (cooperative): defend folding, matador and smash passes with the frame and hip escape.
Then add light resistance.
drills.dosage: 3-4 lengths of the mat; then 3 x 1-min partner rounds
drills.fixes: Flat on the back; shrimping without frames
drills.why: Repetition makes the hip escape automatic so it is available under pressure; the partner progression adds real frames.

drills.name: Guard retention positional rounds
drills.setup: Passer starts standing or kneeling; guard player on back/side.
steps: Passer tries to pass and pin; guard player frames, hip-escapes and reinserts knees/feet.
Reset on a pass or a sweep.
Switch roles each round.
drills.fixes: Flat on the back; shrimping without frames
drills.why: Live but constrained resistance teaches when to frame and move the hips, following Danaher's posture/connection/distance/frames principles.

pro_tips.tip: Guard retention is active distance management - recover guard with knees/shins and chain shrimps as needed.

Carlson Gracie example: when a takedown nearly led to a guard pass, he posted, sat up into a frame, then hip-escaped repeatedly until he could technical stand-up - frame, hip escape, re-guard or stand.

checkpoints.description: Trap one of the mounted opponent's arms (wrist and elbow) and the same-side foot by placing your foot outside theirs.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: both of your hands control one opponent arm; your foot outside the opponent's same-side foot

checkpoints.description: Bridge explosively upward and over the trapped-side shoulder - roll up and over, not sideways.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: hip midpoint rises well above the mat and travels diagonally over the trapped-side shoulder

faults.name: Bridging straight up without trapping
faults.video_signs: Hips go up but opponent posts the arm/leg and stays mounted.
faults.correction_cue: 'Trap the arm AND the foot, then bridge.'
faults.why_it_matters: Without the trap, the opponent simply posts to stop the roll.

faults.name: Rolling sideways
faults.video_signs: Roll goes flat across the mat rather than over the shoulder.
faults.why_it_matters: Rolling sideways loses the momentum of the bridge.

drills.name: Trap-and-roll repetitions
drills.setup: Partner in mount, giving light resistance progressively.
steps: Trap the arm (wrist + elbow) and the same-side foot.
Bridge up and over the trapped-side shoulder.
Land in the partner's guard with posture; reset and repeat both sides.
Progress: partner starts posting/adjusting so timing matters.
drills.why: Repetition with growing resistance grooves the trap-then-bridge order that makes the escape work.

pro_tips.tip: Gracie University teaches the trap-and-roll as the first mount escape in its Combatives curriculum.

checkpoints.description: Head above the hips, spine upright, hips forward/low; hands control hips or biceps rather than posting on the mat.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: trunk within ~30 deg of vertical; head above hip midpoint

faults.name: Posture broken
faults.video_signs: Top player's head is pulled down near the bottom player's chest; hands posted on the mat near the head.
faults.correction_cue: 'Head up, hips in, hands on hips.'
faults.why_it_matters: Broken posture enables triangles, armbars and sweeps.

drills.name: Posture positional rounds
drills.setup: Top player in closed guard; bottom player's only goal is to break posture.
steps: Top: head above hips, hips forward, hands controlling hips/biceps.
Bottom: pull and angle to break posture.
Score a point each time posture is broken; switch roles.
drills.why: Focused resistance trains posture as a reflex before passing is attempted.

pro_tips.tip: Danaher's passing advice starts from posture: you cannot pass well from a broken position.

skills.name: Armbar from closed guard
skills.recommended_camera: Side view perpendicular to the athletes.

checkpoints.description: Control the arm (keep it across your centerline) and climb the guard up high on the opponent's back to create the angle.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: bottom player's hips rotate ~45-90 deg relative to opponent; legs high on the back before extension

checkpoints.description: Finish with hip extension (lifting the hips) while the opponent's thumb points up and elbow is across the hips.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: bottom player's hip rises during finish; opponent elbow joint aligned over the hip line

faults.name: Attacking square / no angle
faults.video_signs: Bottom player stays flat and square; opponent stacks or pulls the arm out.
faults.correction_cue: 'Cut the angle - hip out, climb high.'
faults.why_it_matters: The angle shortens the path to the lever zone.

faults.name: Cranking with the arms only
faults.video_signs: Player pulls the arm without extending the hips.
faults.why_it_matters: Hip/trunk extension provides the finishing force safely and with control.

drills.name: Climb-the-guard armbar drill
drills.setup: Partner kneeling in closed guard, cooperative.
steps: Control the arm across your centerline.
Climb your legs high on the partner's back while cutting your hips to an angle.
Swing the leg over the head and finish slowly with hip extension; partner taps early.
Alternate sides.
drills.dosage: 3 sets x 5 per side, slow finishes
drills.fixes: Attacking square; cranking with arms only
drills.why: Kinematic data show climbing the guard is the shortest path to the lever position; slow finishes keep training partners safe.

pro_tips.tip: In a kinematic study, 'climbing the guard' gave the shortest movement path to the armlock (about half the angular displacement of the foot-on-hip method).
Armbars are a leading mechanism of competition orthopedic injury - apply slowly in training and tap early.

checkpoints.description: Trap one arm in and push one arm out; lock the leg high across the back of the neck.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: choking leg's knee pit behind the opponent's neck (not across the shoulder)

checkpoints.description: Cut an angle (turn ~30-45 deg so you are perpendicular to the opponent), pull the trapped arm across, and break posture by pulling the head down.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: bottom player's hip line rotated ~30-45 deg relative to the opponent's spine

faults.name: Finishing square-on
faults.video_signs: Bottom player faces opponent directly; choke feels loose.
faults.why_it_matters: Square triangles leave space and rely on strength.

faults.name: Posture not broken
faults.video_signs: Opponent sits up tall during the lock.
faults.why_it_matters: A postured opponent can escape or stack.

drills.name: Triangle lock-and-angle drill
drills.setup: Partner kneeling in closed guard, cooperative.
steps: Push one arm out, keep one in; lock the leg high across the back of the neck.
Cut the angle (~30-45 deg) and pull the trapped arm across.
Break posture by pulling the head down; apply slowly.
drills.why: Drilling the angle and posture break makes the finish rely on position rather than strength.

pro_tips.tip: Short legs are not disqualifying for the triangle - angle and arm position matter more than leg length.

checkpoints.description: Post one hand behind, plant the opposite foot, protect the face with the free arm; lift the hips and swing the leg back to stand in base.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: 3 points of contact before lifting; finish in a stance facing forward

faults.name: Standing up forward into the opponent
faults.video_signs: Rises by leaning forward without a post.
faults.why_it_matters: Exposes the head and gives up position.

drills.name: Technical stand-up repetitions
steps: Post hand, plant foot, guard the face with the free hand.
Lift the hips and swing the leg back to base.
Alternate sides.
drills.fixes: Standing up forward into the opponent
drills.why: Repetition on both sides makes the safe stand-up automatic.

pro_tips.tip: The technical stand-up is a core self-defense skill in the Gracie curriculum and should be drilled on both sides.

general_tips.tip: Heel-hook exposure was associated with ~12x higher knee injury incidence in IBJJF brown/black belt competition - teach leg locks only per IBJJF belt/age rules and under supervision.
